subject: Behavioral Economics
title: The Pre-Mortem Technique
description: A 60-second lesson on The Pre-Mortem Technique.

hook.text: Before launching the project, the team imagined it had already failed. Then they asked: why?

buildup.text: Klein's pre-mortem flips optimism bias. Instead of asking what could go right, you start with failure.

discovery.text: This technique surfaces risks people are too polite or optimistic to mention in normal planning.

twist.text: Teams that pre-mortem identify 30% more risks than teams that brainstorm risks the standard way.

climax.text: Starting from failure gives permission to be critical. That permission is the real breakthrough.

punchline.text: Imagine failure first. Prevent it second.

quiz.question: What does a pre-mortem do differently from standard risk planning?
options: It only looks at financial risks
It starts from imagined failure to surface hidden risks

details.summary: A pre-mortem imagines that a project has already failed and asks the team to explain why. This prospective hindsight technique overcomes groupthink and optimism bias by giving permission to voice concerns that would otherwise be suppressed in team settings.
details.whyItMatters: Pre-mortems are one of the most practical debiasing tools for organizational decision-making. By reframing from 'will this work' to 'why did this fail,' teams surface risks that optimism bias and social pressure normally hide.
takeaways: Imagining failure is more productive than asking what could go wrong
Pre-mortems give social permission to voice concerns about team plans
Prospective hindsight generates 30 percent more relevant reasons for failure

faq.question: How do you conduct a pre-mortem?
faq.answer: Before project launch, tell the team to imagine it is one year later and the project has failed spectacularly. Each person independently writes reasons for the failure. Then share and discuss. The failure framing bypasses optimism and groupthink.

faq.question: Why does imagining failure work better than asking about risks?
faq.answer: Asking what could go wrong triggers defensive optimism. Imagining the project has already failed makes identifying problems feel like explaining rather than criticizing. It removes the social cost of being the pessimist in the room.
